OneSpan (OSPN) Q4 2025 Earnings Call Transcript
By

Motley Fool Transcribing

–

Image source: The Motley Fool.


DATE
Feb. 26, 2026 at 4:30 p.m. ET
CALL PARTICIPANTS
Chief Executive Officer — Victor T. Limongelli
Chief Financial Officer — Jorge Martell
Vice President, Investor Relations — Joe Maxa
Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email

TAKEAWAYS
Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR)
-- $187 million at year-end, up 11.5%, with cybersecurity ARR up 12% and digital agreements ARR up 10%.
Q4 Revenue
-- $62.9 million, up 3%, driven by 11% growth in digital agreements and flat performance in cybersecurity.
Full-Year Revenue
-- $243.2 million, unchanged; software and services rose 5.3%, offset by a 16.6% decline in hardware revenue.
Adjusted EBITDA
-- $19 million for Q4 (31% margin) and $78 million annual (32% margin).
Subscription Revenue
-- $38.6 million in Q4 (up 7%); $156.1 million full year (up 12%), with cybersecurity subscription revenue up 13% and digital agreements up 11%.
Profitability
-- Both cybersecurity and digital agreements divisions were profitable for the quarter and full year; Q4 operating income was $12.5 million, up from $11.8 million; full-year operating income was $48.4 million, up from $44.8 million.
Gross Margin
-- 74% for both Q4 and full year, up from 72% for the full year prior period.
Cash Flow
-- $59.5 million in operating cash generated in 2025, with $32 million returned to shareholders through $18.5 million in dividends and $13.1 million in buybacks.
Capital Allocation
-- Completed the Knock Knock and ThreatFabric deals in 2025, and expects Build38 acquisition to close in Q1 2026, all without using its $100 million revolver.
Dividend Policy
-- Quarterly dividend increased from $0.12 to $0.13 per share, annualized to $0.52, reflecting an 8% increase for 2026.
Customer Metrics
-- Net retention rate reached 104% in Q4, up from 103% previously; digital agreements gross retention rate improved by over 4 percentage points, now above 90%.
2026 Outlook
-- Software and services revenue expected at $201 million-$204 million (4%-5% growth); hardware revenue to decline 8%-12% to $43 million-$45 million; total revenue guided to $244 million-$249 million (0%-2% growth); ARR guided to $192 million-$196 million (3%-5% growth); adjusted EBITDA expected at $64 million-$68 million (impacted by Build38 acquisition).
Geographic Revenue Mix
-- Fiscal 2025 (ended Dec. 31, 2025): 42% EMEA, 39% Americas, 19% Asia Pacific; Americas increased, EMEA and Asia Pacific affected by hardware downturns.
Business Model Shift
-- Software now comprises>80% of expected 2026 revenue, with hardware falling below 20%, down sharply from prior years.
SUMMARY
OneSpan

(
OSPN

+0.93%
)
reported a stable top line, meaningful ARR growth, and record profitability, with major cash returns to shareholders and active execution of its software-first strategy. The company disclosed that $3 million of software revenue was recognized in Q4 that would typically have been expected in Q1, impacting upcoming quarterly comparability. Build38’s acquisition, expected to close in the current quarter, will enhance mobile application protection and is projected to dilute adjusted EBITDA by $3 million-$4 million in 2026. Management shared that investments in sales, marketing, and R&D, including a newly hired CRO, are forecast to create revenue acceleration in the second half, although near-term profitability will be pressured. The digital agreements gross retention rate exceeded 90% after a more than 4 percentage point annual improvement, while hardware continues its secular decline, consistent with global mobile banking trends.
Limongelli emphasized a focus on acquiring “technology that is modern and valuable and solves problems,” not targets with existing customer revenue.
Cybersecurity subscription revenue grew 13%, supported by new licenses, client expansion, and M&A, even as total division revenue fell 2.5% annually because of hardware declines.
Digital agreements delivered a 15 percentage point operating income margin improvement year over year, led by new contracts, renewals, and a mix shift to higher-margin services.
Q4’s net retention rate touched 104%, indicating increasing customer engagement and upsell success.
The company stated it remained “solidly profitable” at both division levels, despite notable incremental expenses related to internal investment and M&A activity.
Management said, “The investments we have made recently and those planned for this year are aligned to drive higher software revenue growth in the future and to enable us to achieve long-term sustainable Rule of 40 performance.”
INDUSTRY GLOSSARY
ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue)
: The annualized value of recurring software and subscription contracts recognized at period end, a key SaaS growth indicator.
Rule of 40
: A SaaS industry profitability heuristic stating that a company’s revenue growth rate plus EBITDA margin should equal or exceed 40%.
FIDO2
: An open authentication standard supporting passwordless login, often used with hardware or biometric authenticators in online security.

The second critical area of our cybersecurity value to customers extends beyond authentication into the adjacent area of mobile application protection. Since most consumer banking and a great deal of retail is now conducted via mobile apps, as you know, we have been offering app shielding capabilities for many years, but the threat landscape is evolving rapidly, and we are seeing an increase in sophisticated attacks.
As a result, we recognize that app shielding is a critical area where we need to invest more deeply. To that end, we recently announced a definitive agreement to acquire Build38 to strengthen our app shielding offering. This acquisition will enable deeper integration with our customers' mobile applications and will allow us to dynamically update our detection methods. Over time, it also creates an opportunity to combine the signals detected across our broader mobile portfolio, giving us the ability to deliver richer insights and more robust protection for our customers. In the coming years, we expect the development and growth of consumer AI agents to increase demand by our banking and financial services customers for strong authentication and application protection. In a similar way, the ease by which deepfakes can be created using AI will likely drive demand for secure authentication, which will manifest itself in a variety of ways, including the establishment of digital credentials or wallets by various governments. qa_turns.text: Thank you for your question. Our next question comes from Anja Soderstrom from Sidoti. The floor is yours.

Hi, and thank you for taking my questions, and congrats on the nice progress in the fourth quarter. I am curious, with a new CRO coming on board, what can we expect from him implementing in terms of sales or marketing that you have not done before that you expect to see results from?

Yes, thank you. It is a great question. So just as a reminder, when we went through our restructuring to cut costs, one of the things we did was I was running directly, and having Sean on board is a huge benefit because he is able to focus, you know, full-time, fifty to sixty hours a week, on sales execution, on pipeline development, on review of any accounts that may be at risk. So the ability to really add focus and discipline, I think, is one of the things we are going to see from Sean. And then he also owns all of go to market, so improving our lead generation, leading to pipeline, ultimately leading to closed business.
Of course, that will take a while. As I mentioned, six- to nine-month sales cycle, sometimes longer. But we expect to see improvements in all those areas over time.

Okay. Thank you. And then, in terms of the acquisition of Build38, how did that come about? And how should we think about further M&A opportunities? Are there any sort of capabilities that you currently feel that you are missing, that you are actively looking, that might help you accelerate?

Yeah. Let me address that a little bit. Strategically, what we are trying to do with these acquisitions is find good, valuable technology that could solve problems for our customers, ideally in our core areas and things like authentication or app shielding. We are not looking to buy customers, so we are not looking to buy revenue. We are looking to buy technology that is modern and valuable and solves problems, and then we have a lot of customers, and then ultimately sell that to our customers and new customers as well, and therefore take that technology and get it more widely distributed. That is the goal.
So both of these companies, Knock and Build38, really were not—they did not have a ton of revenue—but they had spent a lot of time and a lot of investment building great technology, and that is really what we are looking for.
Okay. Thank you. And just one last one, as we have all this AI discussion now, how do you see AI as an opportunity for OneSpan Inc., or also maybe as a potential threat?

Thanks, Anja. Obviously, this has been all over the news in the software market over in 2026. A couple of things. When you look at areas like app shielding, it is really cutting edge. If you are taking existing code and you are building an application shielding offering, you know, next week, next month, the month after that, there are new cutting-edge exploits that you have to be on top of. So if we get to AGI, it is a totally different story. But the way things stand now, we think that is fairly well insulated.
And even things like authentication—these are critical consumer interactions enabling them to do business—and it just seems like the risk is super high for somebody to try to build their own. On the opportunity side, you have things that are not so common now but will likely be common over the next three to four years of consumers employing agents to interact with their banks, to do shopping in retail, and that is going to increase the need for authentication far above what it is today. So, over the longer run, we think there is going to be quite a bit of opportunity to deliver more value.
